ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | Austin, TX
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Austin, TX: wall thickness surveys on plant piping and vessels, plus angle-beam weld UT on structural steel. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Gauging in Austin, Texas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Austin work sites for ultrasonic thickness gauging on process piping, vessels and tanks, and for shear-wave ultrasonic weld inspection on structural and pressure-boundary steel. Typical Austin jobs include chilled-water and cooling loops at chip fabs and data centers, gas-fired generating equipment, water treatment piping and steel erection. Tell us the component, the code and the access, and request a UT inspection quote for Austin.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Austin

Austin is a different kind of industrial city from the Gulf Coast refining towns. Its heavy industry is built around semiconductor manufacturing, which brought fabrication plants, ultrapure water systems, chemical delivery and large mechanical rooms to the region, along with a continuing wave of data center construction. Utilities add gas-fired generating stations, and the city and county run water and wastewater treatment plants with large-diameter steel piping. Highway reconstruction in the Austin area means steel bridge girders and sign structures.

Each of these has an ultrasonic job in it. A fab's utility plant has carbon steel chilled-water and condenser-water piping that thins at elbows and dead legs. A generating station has boiler tubes, steam piping and feedwater lines where wall loss is tracked for years. A water plant has buried and exposed steel mains. A steel building under erection has complete-joint-penetration groove welds on columns and beams that a design drawing marks for volumetric examination. Austin hosts all of them within one metro area, so the same technician skill set gets used on very different assets.

What UT measures in Austin plants, and what it does not

Ultrasonic testing sends high-frequency sound into the part and times the echo. For thickness work, the technician couples a probe to the outside surface and reads the time the sound takes to reach the back wall and return; with the velocity set for the material, the instrument displays remaining wall. That gives a direct reading of internal corrosion or erosion from the outside while the line stays in service. It works on carbon steel, stainless, aluminum and most other metals that transmit sound.

The limits matter just as much. Heavy external scale, blistered paint, or a rough pitted surface scatters the sound, so the probe location has to be cleaned first. Corrosion that is narrow and deep can be missed between readings, so a single number at a condition monitoring location says nothing about the pipe a foot away. Coarse-grained cast or austenitic stainless material attenuates the beam. For welds, ultrasonics finds planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks very well, but the weld geometry, backing bars and thin sections require a technique written for the joint, not a generic scan.

Codes that govern ultrasonic work in Austin

The code that applies depends on the asset. For plant piping, ASME B31.3 sets examination requirements, and for power piping ASME B31.1 applies. Pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Appendix 12 for ultrasonic examination of welds. Method requirements come from ASME Section V: Article 4 covers ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 5 covers materials, and Article 23 carries the contact thickness measurement standard SE-797. ASTM E797 is the matching practice for pulse-echo thickness measurement, and ASTM E164 covers contact ultrasonic examination of weldments.

Structural steel for buildings falls under AWS D1.1, which includes ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, while state highway bridge steel is welded and inspected under AWS D1.5. The owner decides which edition governs the contract, and we work to the edition named in the specification.

Texas also has its own regime for steam equipment. The state's Boiler Program, run by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, registers non-exempt boilers and requires certificates of operation, and insured boilers are inspected by the insurer or its designee. That inspection belongs to the commissioned inspector. Our thickness data goes to the owner and the inspector as supporting evidence for their decision. Where a mechanical integrity program is run under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j), our readings feed the owner's inspection plan, and the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for any API 510, 570 or 653 conclusions.

How a thickness survey is carried out

A good survey starts with a plan, not a probe. The owner or inspector identifies condition monitoring locations (CMLs) on isometrics or equipment drawings, and the technician grids each one. On pipe, readings are normally taken around the circumference at an elbow or reducer, not only at the top of the pipe, because internal flow concentrates attack on the outside radius or at the six o'clock position.

The technician calibrates a dual-element probe on a step block of the same alloy as the part, then verifies the setup on a known thickness before and after the work. Dual-element probes handle rough, corroded surfaces better than single-crystal contact probes because the transmit and receive crystals are separated and angled. On pitted surfaces we watch the A-scan display, not only the digital number, since a gauge in digital mode can lock on a false echo or double the thickness on a thin wall.

Hot lines are common in utility plants. A high-temperature probe and couplant rated for the surface are used, the calibration is made at or corrected for temperature, and the technician records the surface temperature with the reading. Results are logged against the CML identifier so next year's survey can be compared point by point and a corrosion rate calculated by the owner's inspector.

Shear-wave weld examination on structural and pressure steel

For groove welds the technician uses an angle-beam probe, usually 45, 60 or 70 degrees, and builds a reference level from side-drilled holes in a calibration block or a distance-amplitude curve, as the written procedure specifies. The probe is moved in a raster pattern beside the weld to cover the weld and heat-affected zone from both sides where access allows. Indications are evaluated for length, amplitude relative to the reference and position in the thickness, then compared with the acceptance criteria in the governing code.

Weld UT is a good fit in Austin for column splices and moment connections on steel-framed buildings, where the specification lists specific joints for volumetric examination, and for butt welds in thick-wall piping and vessel shells. It does not replace a visual examination, and on thin sections or tricky geometry a code may require another method instead. Whether ultrasonic examination can stand in for another volumetric method on a given job is a question for the owner, the engineer of record and the inspector before work begins.

Who performs the work and who reviews it

Atlantis technicians who perform ultrasonic examination are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II technician calibrates the instrument, scans the component and judges what the screen shows. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the reporting, so a second qualified person reads the work before it reaches you. Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer certifies its personnel; a course provider does not, and a training certificate by itself does not authorize anyone to sign a report. If your own written practice has special requirements, our Level III can review them through our Level III consulting service, and if you need a written practice drafted we cover that under written practice development.

What the UT report contains

Each report names the component and its location, the procedure number and revision, the governing code and edition, and the acceptance criteria used. It lists the instrument, probe, calibration block and couplant, the calibration results, the technician's name and level, and the date. For thickness work it includes a grid or table with the nominal thickness, the minimum required thickness where the owner supplies it, and each reading with its location. For welds it gives each recordable indication with its position, length, amplitude and the accept or reject call. A sketch or photograph of the scan area is attached so a reviewer can find the same spot a year later.

Planning ultrasonic work in Austin

Central Texas summers shape the schedule. Steel in direct sun reaches temperatures far above air temperature, so probes and couplant are chosen for the surface, and technicians are given breaks and shade under the site's heat rules. Winter is usually mild, so cold-weather limits on couplant seldom govern, though a norther can drop temperatures quickly. Humidity and thunderstorms occasionally interrupt outdoor scanning, and wet surfaces need a dry, clean scan area to hold calibration.

Many Austin sites require badging, safety orientation and sometimes security screening before a technician reaches the unit, and chip fabs and data centers add clean-room or gowning rules and escort requirements. Tell us early about hot work permits, confined space entry for tank and vessel work, and any contractor safety program such as ISNetworld-type registrations. We mobilize from outside the city, so travel and lodging are planned with the scope. We reply within one business day to a quote request, and the schedule is set once the scope and access are agreed.

Ultrasonic, magnetic particle and liquid penetrant: choosing for Austin jobs

Use ultrasonics when the question is remaining wall thickness or a flaw buried in the weld. Use magnetic particle inspection in Austin when the concern is a surface crack in carbon or low-alloy steel, such as a toe crack on a crane runway or a lifting lug. Use liquid penetrant testing in Austin when the material is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic metal, or when you need to check a repaired surface of any material for cracks open to the surface. Thickness mapping and crack detection answer different questions, so many Austin jobs pair two methods on the same weld.

For national background on the method, see our ultrasonic testing service page and the ultrasonic testing guide. For code details on thickness gauging, read our summary of ASME Section V thickness requirements.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians in Austin

If your Austin facility would rather qualify its own people, our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training cover the theory and practical preparation, with the ultrasonic testing simulator for practice before hands-on time. See the NDT training page for Austin and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker for experience hours.

faq.q: How is an ultrasonic thickness survey quoted for an Austin plant?
faq.a: The quote follows the scope: number of condition monitoring locations, surface condition, temperature, access and travel. Send your drawings or CML list through the quote link and we reply within one business day with the questions we need answered.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be done while the line is running?
faq.a: Yes. Thickness gauging is done from the outside surface while the equipment stays in service, as long as the surface is safe to reach and a probe and couplant suited to the temperature are used. Hot work and entry permits depend on your site.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Austin?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Austin. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so travel and site access are planned together with the inspection.

faq.q: Which codes do you use for ultrasonic weld inspection in Austin?
faq.a: We work to the code your specification names: ASME Section V Article 4 with Section VIII Appendix 12 or B31.3 for pressure equipment and piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural steel groove welds. State bridge work follows AWS D1.5.

faq.q: Do I need an authorized inspector for ultrasonic work on pressure equipment?
faq.a: For equipment under API 510, 570 or 653, or the Texas boiler rules, the owner’s authorized or commissioned inspector remains responsible. We perform the examination and give that inspector the thickness and indication data.

faq.q: How accurate is ultrasonic thickness gauging on pitted or painted surfaces?
faq.a: Accuracy depends on calibration on the same alloy, a clean surface and a dual-element probe, and the technician watches the A-scan to avoid false echoes. Heavy pitting may need extra readings or surface preparation.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic weld inspection replace another volumetric method on my project?
faq.a: Only when the construction code and the owner both allow it. The substitution is agreed in advance with the engineer of record and the authorized inspector, because the acceptance criteria differ between methods.

faq.q: What information should I send to get a UT quote for Austin?
faq.a: Send the component list or drawings, materials and thickness range, surface temperature, governing code and edition, access conditions, site badging needs and the target window. Photographs of the surfaces help us plan.

faq.q: Can you train our Austin staff to do their own thickness gauging?
faq.a: Yes. Our UT Level 1 and Level 2 training prepares your technicians under SNT-TC-1A, and your company then certifies them under its own written practice after the required experience hours.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Austin, TX | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MT) in Austin, TX for weld toes, lugs, crane steel and forgings. Yoke and prod mag particle testing. Ask for a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Austin, Texas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Austin facilities and job sites for magnetic particle inspection of welds, lifting hardware, crane steel and machined parts. MT finds surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel, which makes it a fast check on structural welds, lifting lugs and repaired surfaces. State what you need examined and where, then request a magnetic particle inspection quote for Austin.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Austin

Austin's economy is more about high-technology construction and manufacturing than refining, and that shapes the steel work. Large chip fabs and data centers are built on structural steel frames with heavy crane loads during erection, and those cranes, rigging lugs and spreader beams are lifted repeatedly. Equipment manufacturers in the region fabricate frames, skids and pressure parts. Power generation equipment, water treatment structures and highway bridge steel round out the list. Every one of those sites has welded carbon or low-alloy steel where the failure mode is a surface crack that starts at a weld toe or a sharp notch.

Typical Austin jobs for MT include weld toes on column splices and bracing connections, padeyes and lifting lugs added for equipment setting, crane runway beams and hook blocks, trailer and truck frame repairs, and weld repairs made after a gouged-out defect. When a structural drawing calls for surface examination of a fillet weld, or a rigging inspector wants proof that a lug weld is crack-free before a heavy lift, magnetic particle testing is usually the quickest answer.

What MT finds, and where it cannot help

Magnetic particle inspection works on ferromagnetic materials only: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades. When the part is magnetized, a crack or other break in the surface interrupts the magnetic field and pulls fine iron particles into a visible line. The method is sensitive to tight surface cracks that a visual examination could miss, and it also reveals some discontinuities just under the surface.

It will not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or titanium, because they do not carry a magnetic field. Austin facilities with stainless process piping need liquid penetrant testing in Austin for those welds instead. MT is also not a depth gauge: it shows that a crack exists and where it runs, not how deep it is, and it cannot find a flaw buried deep in a thick weld. Paint or scale thick enough to keep particles from reaching the metal has to be removed before an examination.

Codes and acceptance criteria

The method itself is governed by ASME Section V, Article 7, with ASTM E709 as the general guide and ASTM E1444 as the practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code: for pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 gives the MT methods and acceptance standards, and for process piping ASME B31.3 sections 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 apply. Structural steel under AWS D1.1 uses its own surface examination provisions, and state highway bridges built under AWS D1.5 follow the bridge code.

In Texas, the Boiler Program at the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation oversees registered boilers and certifies repair and alteration companies, so MT of a boiler repair weld is reported to the owner and the commissioned inspector. Mechanical integrity programs under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) also expect recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. Read our breakdown of Article 7 requirements for the detail behind a procedure.

How the technique is applied

For most Austin field work the technician uses an electromagnetic yoke. The yoke is placed across the weld, the particles are applied, and indications are read and recorded. Under Article 7, an AC yoke must show a minimum lifting power of 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke 40 pounds, checked on a test piece before the work begins. The part is examined at least twice, with the field turned roughly 90 degrees between passes, so that cracks running in any direction are crossed by the field.

Dry powder is convenient on rough weld surfaces in warm weather, while wet visible or fluorescent particles are more sensitive on smooth machined parts. Fluorescent work needs a darkened area and a UV-A light with the intensity and ambient-white-light limits the procedure sets, which on a bright Texas jobsite usually means a tent or a covered, shaded work area. Prods can be used for thick sections where a yoke does not reach, but burn marks on the surface make them unsuitable for some finished parts, so the procedure states when they are allowed.

Where residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining or a sensitive instrument, the part is demagnetized and checked with a field indicator afterward. Magnetized ferromagnetic structure near arc welding can also deflect the arc, which is another reason to demagnetize.

Who does the work and how it is reviewed

MT technicians who work for Atlantis are qualified under our written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II adjusts the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the indications against the code. An ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and the reporting format, giving you a second qualified reviewer on the process. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer issues the certification, so the written practice of the technician's employer is what defines what he or she can sign. If you need a procedure written for your own project or want a Level III to audit a contractor's MT work, see our Level III consulting service and written practice development.

Structural erection and rigging checks around Austin

A large share of Austin MT work comes from construction rather than plant maintenance. When a steel frame goes up for a fab, a data center or an office tower, erectors weld temporary lifting lugs, shear plates and bracing, and some of those welds are ground off afterward. Crane picks of heavy equipment rely on padeyes and spreader beams whose welds the rigging engineer may require to be crack-free. A quick pass with a yoke before the lift gives the rigger documented evidence instead of a visual opinion. For permanent connections, a project specification may list a percentage of fillet welds on moment frames for surface examination, and the technician works from the weld map the special inspector provides.

Weld repairs bring another need. After a defect is excavated by grinding or air-arc gouging, MT confirms the cavity is clear before the repair weld is made, and again after the repair is ground flush. Skipping the first check means welding over a crack tip that was not fully removed, which is a common reason for a repair to fail. The report ties each check to the repair record so the sequence is visible to the inspector.

Telling cracks from look-alikes

A line of collected powder does not always mean a crack. Sharp changes of section, the edge of a weld cap, a scribe mark or a magnetic writing on the steel can hold particles. A trained Level II tells relevant indications from non-relevant ones by looking at shape and position, lightly dressing the area and re-examining, or changing the field direction. A tight crack gives a sharp, crisp line that persists after the particles are blown away and rebuilt, while a magnetic-writing indication fades after demagnetizing and repeats poorly. Rounded indications are evaluated differently from linear ones under most acceptance tables, and the report states which category each falls under.

Surface condition affects what can be seen. A weld left in the as-welded condition with spatter and a rough toe will hold particles that mimic defects, so a light grind or wire-brush of the area is agreed before the examination. Coatings thicker than the procedure permits must be removed, because the field has to reach the steel at full strength.

What the MT report shows

Every report identifies the part or weld by drawing number or tag, the procedure and revision, and the code edition. It records the magnetizing technique, yoke or prod spacing, the lifting power check, the particles and carrier used, the lighting measurements for fluorescent work and the technician's name and level. Each indication is listed with its location, orientation and length, and is marked accepted or rejected against the named criteria. Sketches or photos show the extent of the area examined, and any demagnetization result is noted.

Planning MT work in Austin

Surface temperature is a practical issue in Central Texas. Steel left in summer sun can be too hot for some particle suspensions and for a technician's hand, and when the surface exceeds the range the procedure permits, the work either waits for the part to cool or uses a procedure qualified for the higher temperature. Cold is rarely a limit here, but wet weather and wind can blow dry powder away or ruin a wet bath, so outdoor work is often scheduled for dry mornings and shielded where possible.

Plan for site access: badging, safety orientation, hot work and lift permits, and the clean-area or escort rules at fabs and data centers. Because Atlantis has no office in Austin, technicians are mobilized to your site, so you will want to combine the MT scope with any other inspection so the trip serves the whole job. We reply within one business day to a quote request.

MT, PT or UT for your Austin job

Pick MT for ferromagnetic steel when the target is a surface crack. If the material is stainless or aluminum, or the surface cannot take a magnetic field, choose liquid penetrant in Austin. If you need to know wall thickness or look for a buried flaw, choose ultrasonic testing in Austin. Many repairs get MT on the final weld and ultrasonics on the base metal around it. Our comparison of MT and PT explains the choice in more detail, and the national magnetic particle testing page and MT guide cover the basics.

Training your own MT technicians in Austin

Companies in the Austin area that want in-house capability can start with our MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, then use the Austin NDT training page and practice tests to prepare for the employer's examinations.

faq.q: What can magnetic particle inspection find on structural steel in Austin?
faq.a: MT finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks, laps and seams in ferromagnetic steel, such as toe cracks on welds, cracks at lifting lugs and fatigue cracks on crane steel. It does not show depth and will not detect deep buried flaws.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel pipe at an Austin fab?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless does not hold a magnetic field, which rules MT out for it. Liquid penetrant testing is the normal choice for surface cracks in stainless welds, and ultrasonics covers thickness or buried flaws.

faq.q: Do you perform fluorescent magnetic particle testing outdoors?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles need a darkened work area and a UV-A light with the intensity the procedure sets. On a sunny jobsite we use a shelter or tent, or choose visible-color particles where the procedure allows them.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep a team in Austin for MT work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Austin. Qualified technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, which is why we ask for the full list of components and access conditions when you request a quote.

faq.q: Which standard do you use for MT acceptance?
faq.a: We use the acceptance criteria of the construction code your project names, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 or B31.3 for pressure equipment and piping, or AWS D1.1 for structural welds. The procedure cites the edition.

faq.q: Why does magnetic particle inspection require two directions of magnetization?
faq.a: Cracks are only revealed when they cross the magnetic field at a good angle. Examining twice, about ninety degrees apart, catches cracks that run in any direction on the surface.

faq.q: Do parts need to be demagnetized after MT?
faq.a: Only when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, instruments or service. When it is required, the technician demagnetizes the part and verifies the field with a meter before reporting.

faq.q: What do I send to get an MT quote for Austin?
faq.a: Send the list of components or welds, material grade, surface condition and coating, size range, applicable code and edition, access and permit needs, and preferred timing. A few photos make planning easier.

faq.q: Can our own technicians learn MT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. We offer MT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A. Your company then qualifies and certifies its technicians under its own written practice after the required experience.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Austin, TX | Dye Check
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection in Austin, TX for stainless piping, aluminum and repaired welds. Mobilized crews. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Austin, Texas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing in Austin for welds and machined surfaces in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and any other non-porous material. Dye penetrant inspection is the practical choice where magnetic methods cannot work, such as ultrapure process piping, cleanroom tooling and pressure parts. Describe the components and the code, and request a penetrant testing quote for Austin.

Where liquid penetrant testing fits in Austin

Austin's chip-making cluster is the reason penetrant work matters here. Semiconductor fabs and their suppliers rely on stainless steel process piping for gases, chemicals and ultrapure water, and on welded stainless and aluminum chambers, frames and enclosures. These materials are not magnetic, so a surface crack in a weld has to be found by penetrant rather than magnetic particles. The same applies to aluminum structures, cryogenic and heat-exchanger components, and the stainless piping in food, beverage and pharmaceutical plants around Central Texas.

Power and water systems add more PT work: stainless heat recovery components, chemical feed piping at treatment plants, and weld repairs on pumps and valves. On carbon steel, penetrant is used when magnetic particle inspection is awkward, for example inside a small bore, on a thin section or on a part with a complex shape. Because penetrant finds only flaws that are open to the surface, it is usually a final-surface check after grinding, machining or repair, not a way to look inside a weld.

What PT finds and what it cannot find

The method depends on capillary action. A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean surface and drawn into any surface-breaking crack, pore or lap. After the excess is removed, a developer pulls the trapped liquid back out, producing a visible indication much wider than the flaw itself. Visible red dye is read under normal white light, while fluorescent penetrant is read under UV-A light in a dim area and is more sensitive for tight cracks.

The key limit is that the flaw must be open to the surface. Anything smeared over by grinding, peening, buffing or heavy blasting can be closed, and a flaw packed with oil, paint or corrosion product will not take penetrant. Porous materials and very rough surfaces give broad false indications. PT also cannot size depth. If the question is remaining wall or an internal flaw, the answer lies with ultrasonic testing in Austin, and for crack detection in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Austin is often quicker.

Codes, procedures and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 6 governs the method, ASTM E165 provides the general-industry practice, and ASTM E1417 applies to some other work. For pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 supplies the PT methods and acceptance, while process piping follows ASME B31.3 section 344.4 with the acceptance table in 341.3.2. Power piping uses B31.1. Welded stainless and other alloy work for structural steel goes to AWS D1.1 or AWS D1.6, depending on the material.

The procedure also controls the penetrant materials. Under ASME Section V, the sulfur and halogen content of the materials has to be controlled when they will be used on nickel-base alloys and austenitic stainless steel, because residues can cause damage later. A material lot certification is part of the paperwork for those jobs. Read our Article 6 explanation for the detail behind each requirement. In Texas, repairs on registered boilers fall under the state's boiler rules and the commissioned inspector, with our results given to them for their decision.

How a penetrant examination is done

Surface preparation decides the result. The technician cleans the area with a solvent cleaner or detergent, removes scale, slag and spatter, and lets the part dry fully. Light grinding can be used if the surface is smeared, but a chemical etch may be needed after heavy machining or blasting to reopen the flaws, and the procedure states when. Cleaning must be complete, because oil in a crack will block the penetrant.

The penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion and left for the dwell time the procedure sets, which depends on the material, the flaw type and the temperature. Excess is removed with solvent-dampened cloths for the solvent-removable method, or with a controlled water rinse for water-washable systems. Over-washing can pull penetrant out of shallow flaws. A thin, even coat of developer is then applied and the surface is read after the development time, with the area checked again for a second look as indications grow.

Technicians keep a record of the penetrant, remover and developer by brand and lot, the dwell and development times and the surface temperature. Comparator blocks or other checks verify that the materials are performing as expected before a job starts.

Temperature and weather in Central Texas

ASME Section V sets a standard operating window of about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Outside that window the procedure has to be demonstrated at the temperature actually used. That matters in Austin more than in many places: a stainless pipe or aluminum panel in direct summer sun can exceed the upper end of the window while the air temperature feels merely hot, and a hot surface makes solvent penetrant dry and evaporate before it can enter a flaw. On those days work is moved to early morning, shaded or cooled, or run with a procedure qualified for the higher range.

Winter nights occasionally dip close to the lower end, and wet weather can wash away penetrant or dilute the developer. In the cleanroom or fab setting, expect restrictions on solvents, aerosols and wipes, and ask for approved low-residue materials in advance.

False indications and how they are resolved

Penetrant produces its own kinds of misleading marks. Bleed-out from a weld pit or a rough toe can look like a crack, residual penetrant left in a threaded area can leave a pattern, and an under-cleaned surface develops a pink or glowing background that hides real flaws. The technician judges an indication by its shape and by how it grows during the development time, wipes it away with a solvent-dampened swab, and re-develops the spot to see whether it returns in the same place. A line that reappears sharply and straight is evaluated as a crack, while a broad diffuse stain that does not return is classed as non-relevant and documented as such.

When indications are marginal, the Level II can request a re-clean and a repeat examination, or the Level III can review the photographs. Honest reporting of non-relevant marks is part of the record, because a reviewer reading the report later needs to know the area was not ignored.

Process piping and tooling in Austin's high-technology plants

High-purity systems have rules that general industrial work does not. Welded stainless gas lines and ultrapure water headers must stay clean on the inside, so penetrant work is limited to the outside surface of the weld unless the owner specifies otherwise, and the cleaning chemicals must be approved by the facility. Owners may have tight limits on residue and on contact with materials that could contaminate a clean system, so the procedure is reviewed and approved before the technician goes near the line. Aluminum chambers, stainless tool frames and welded enclosures follow the same principle: check the surface, record the lot numbers and leave no residue.

For fabrication shops serving this market, PT is also a common final check on machined stainless and aluminum components, on repaired casting surfaces and on weld overlays. The result is a clear surface record before assembly, which is easier to correct than a leak found after installation.

Documentation is part of the job on regulated Texas work. If the weld is on equipment registered with the state, the owner's file needs the examination record, and our report is written so the commissioned inspector can attach it without rework. Owners who run mechanical integrity programs keep these records as evidence that inspection followed the written program, so a photograph of each prepared surface and the final indication map adds real value later.

Who performs and reviews the work

Penetrant examinations are carried out by technicians qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II prepares the surface, performs the test and evaluates the indications. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and checks the report format, adding a second qualified reviewer. The certifying authority under SNT-TC-1A is the employer, and the written practice defines exactly what each technician is allowed to do. Our Level III consulting and written practice development services are available if you need a procedure for a specific project or an audit of someone else's PT.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the part or weld, the procedure and revision, the code and acceptance criteria, and the examiner's name and level. It lists the penetrant type and method, the cleaner, remover and developer with lot numbers, the surface temperature, the dwell and development times and the light measurements for fluorescent work. Each indication is described by location, shape and size, with a note on whether it is relevant, linear or rounded, and whether it is accepted or rejected. Photographs and sketches of the area and the final cleaning step are included so the reviewer can follow the examination.

Choosing between PT, MT and UT in Austin

Penetrant is the right call for non-magnetic alloys and for a check of a repaired surface in any material. Choose MT where the steel is magnetic and speed or sensitivity just under the surface counts, and ultrasonics where wall thickness or buried flaws matter. Our MT versus PT comparison sets out the tradeoffs, and the national penetrant testing page gives background on the method.

faq.q: When should I use liquid penetrant instead of magnetic particle in Austin?
faq.a: Use penetrant when the material is non-magnetic, such as stainless steel, aluminum or nickel alloys, or when the shape or finish makes magnetizing impractical. Magnetic particle is usually quicker on carbon steel weld surfaces.

faq.q: Can PT find cracks under paint or scale?
faq.a: No. The flaw must be open to the surface and the surface must be clean. Paint, scale, oil or smeared metal can hide a crack, so the area is cleaned and sometimes etched before the penetrant is applied.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard range under ASME Section V is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Hot Austin surfaces in summer sun can exceed it, so the work is shifted, shaded, or run under a procedure qualified for the actual temperature.

faq.q: Do you use low-halogen penetrant on stainless steel?
faq.a: When the code or specification requires it, such as for austenitic stainless or nickel alloys, we use materials with controlled sulfur and halogen content and record the lot certification in the report.

faq.q: Which codes cover penetrant inspection of pressure parts?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 governs the method, with acceptance from Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels or B31.3 for process piping. The procedure names the exact edition used on the job.

faq.q: Is fluorescent penetrant better than visible dye?
faq.a: Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive to fine cracks but needs a darkened area and UV-A light. Visible dye works in normal light and is simpler in the field. The procedure sets which is allowed for the component.

faq.q: How should I prepare a surface before the technician arrives?
faq.a: Remove loose scale, paint, grease and spatter in the test area if you can, and keep the surface dry. The technician completes the final cleaning, and the procedure states when grinding or etching is also needed.
